items.excerpt: 2026-11-09 08:18:15 Death toll from Egypt's train collision rises to 7, with 112 injured The death toll from Sunday's collision between two trains in Egypt's Giza governorate has risen to seven, with 112 others injured, Egypt's Ministry of Health and Population said. The ministry said in a statement that 45 patients had been discharged after their conditions improved and they received the necessary treatment, while seven others were expected to be discharged soon. The remaining injured were continuing to receive treatment under medical observation. Earlier in the day, the ministry said in another statement that 72 ambulances took part in rescue and evacuation operations, with the injured transferred to multiple hospitals in Giza and nearby Beni Suef governorate. Israeli opposition leader Eisenkot officially receives mandate to form gov't Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Sunday formally tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government, giving the former military chief a chance to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after his right-wing coalition lost its parliamentary majority in October's election. Eisenkot, leader of the centrist Yashar party, received recommendations from 67 lawmakers in the 120-seat parliament, against 46 for Netanyahu. At the ceremony, Herzog called for a "stable government that can last" and called for unity. South Africa's ANC remains largest party despite vote decline South Africa's ruling African National Congress (ANC) retained its position as the country's largest political party in the 2026 local government elections despite a sharp decline in voter support. The results released by the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) on Sunday showed that the ANC, led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, received 30.76 percent of the votes counted nationwide, down more than 14 percentage points from the previous local elections in 2021. The ANC's main rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), secured 24.64 percent. The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, won 9.76 percent in its first contest in local government elections. Trump says renewed strikes on Iran "highly unlikely" if talks progress U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that renewed military strikes on Iran were "highly unlikely" as long as negotiations made progress, but did not rule out further military actions. In a phone interview with CNN, Trump claimed that the United States had already dealt a severe blow to Iran and that further military action was "highly unlikely" to be necessary. "It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," Trump noted, referring to Iran's nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Yemen's Houthis claim missile, drone strikes on Saudi oil facilities, Riyadh airport Yemen's Houthi group said Sunday that it had launched four military operations involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones against an international airport and a financial center in the Saudi capital Riyadh, oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, as well as troop positions inside Yemen, claiming extensive damage and casualties. In a statement aired by the group's al-Masirah TV, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the first operation targeted King Khalid International Airport, Saudi energy giant Aramco's oil storage tanks and a financial center in Riyadh, claiming direct hits and significant damage.

items.excerpt: ## US Democrats plan probes of Musk, Miller, corporate America after midterm rout Tech megabillionaire Elon Musk and President Donald Trump’s newly appointed White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, and some large companies will likely be targets of congressional probes when Democrats take control of Congress in January, senior lawmakers said on Nov 8. In television appearances, US Representative Robert Garcia of California and US Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, set to lead the House Oversight and Senate Banking committees, vowed aggressive oversight after their party’s sweeping midterm election victory. Meanwhile, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries indicated he and his fellow Democrats would back an impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Garcia, who is the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said investigations will focus on Musk’s involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency’s firing of federal workers in 2025, and Miller’s role in Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown. ## Nvidia opens probe after report of CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy PHOTO: REUTERS Nvidia said on Nov 8 it is initiating an independent investigation after a media report alleged CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. In a message to Nvidia employees, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and took “full responsibility” for his actions. The New York Times reported in October that the US authorities were investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. ## Hacked records show 400,000 Russians killed in war on Ukraine PHOTO: AFP Russia has recorded the deaths of about 400,000 of its people fighting in Ukraine since the full-scale invasion almost five years ago, according to confidential data held by the country’s statistics agency, Rosstat. The information comes from more than 11 million death certificates with accompanying details such as residence, age and where people died. The data was obtained by the Belarusian pro-opposition group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacker operation Silent Crow. It was subsequently shared with Bloomberg News and a small group of other outlets. Between Feb 24, 2022, and late August 2026, almost 392,700 death certificates in the data explicitly link the fatalities to the war, either via coding or freeform text fields mentioning terms such as “military operation,” “shelling” or “drones.”

items.title: ECONOMIC WEEK AHEAD: November 9-13
items.excerpt: (2) Fedspeak. Ten Fed officials are scheduled to speak this week (Goolsbee, Barkin, Waller, Logan, Schmid, Paulson, Hammack, Daly, Williams, and Jefferson). These are their first remarks after the Democratic sweep. These Fed heads are likely hawkish on balance, especially after Friday's strong employment report. In early October, the federal funds rate (FFR) futures implied 3.3 rate hikes over the next 12 months and 1.7 over the next six. Since then, those projections have fallen to 1.9 and 1.4 (chart). Friday’s employment report lifted the odds of a December rate hike to 78%. We think the FOMC still needs another 50bps of increases to reach a neutral FFR. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly told CNBC on Friday that “the job market remains stable and solid, but not booming,” with real wages falling as pay lags inflation. She expects the Fed “will have to tighten policy further.” (3) Inflation. October’s CPI and PPI reports will be released on Tuesday and Friday, respectively. The Cleveland Fed’s Inflation Nowcasting model projects that the headline CPI rose 0.24% m/m and the core CPI 0.21% m/m. That would hold headline CPI inflation at 3.7% y/y and ease core to 2.5% from 2.6% (chart). October would mark the 68th consecutive month of CPI inflation above 2.0% y/y. The model sees both accelerating in November, to 3.9% and 2.8% y/y. The Nowcast also suggests that October’s PCED inflation will remain firmly above the Fed’s 2.0% target, with the headline and core PCED inflation rates projected at 3.8% y/y and 3.2% y/y, respectively. Both are expected to heat up a bit in November. October's PPI inflation is likely to be hotter than September's headline and core readings of 6.3% and 5.0% (chart). One of the more troublesome components of the PPI recently has been transportation & warehousing services, which jumped 16.0% y/y in September (chart). Soaring diesel prices are fueling inflation. (4) ADP & unemployment claims. Payrolls rose 165,000 in October, well above the 65,000 consensus. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%. ADP’s weekly employment reading (Tue) follows a four-week average of 16,750 for the week ended October 10, down from 17,500 (chart). ADP’s monthly report showed private payrolls up 86,000 in October, beating the 67,000 consensus. Initial jobless claims (Thu) follow last week's 189,000, with the four-week average falling to 194,750, the lowest since 1969 (chart). Continuing claims were 1,718,000 for the week ended October 23, with a four-week average of 1,709,000.

items.excerpt: November 8, 2026 US inflation accelerated in September, while economic growth exceeded expectations in the third quarter and jobless claims remained near multi-decade lows, presenting the Federal Reserve with a challenging policy outlook. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the central bank’s preferred inflation gauge, increased 0.5% month-on-month on a seasonally adjusted basis, taking the annual rate to 3.6%, according to Commerce Department data released Thursday. The monthly increase matched the Dow Jones consensus forecast, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below expectations. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% from the previous month and 3.1% annually. Both readings were in line with economists’ forecasts. Fed officials generally view core inflation as a better indicator of longer-term price pressures, although they monitor both measures. Inflation remains significantly above the Fed’s 2% target, even as the economy continues to demonstrate resilience. ## Economic growth exceeds expectations The Commerce Department report showed that US gross domestic product increased at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, beating the 3.1% estimate and accelerating from 2.2% growth in the second quarter. Consumer spending, a key driver of the US economy, increased 0.5% in September, slightly below the 0.6% gain forecast by economists. Personal income rose 0.2%, compared with expectations for a 0.3% increase. The combination of firm economic growth and persistent inflation could make it harder for policymakers to justify easing monetary policy in the near term. The data arrived a day after the Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75%-4.00%. Officials have said they can assess incoming economic information before deciding on their next move, despite inflation remaining elevated.

items.title: McCormick calls for delay in Senate GOP leadership elections
items.excerpt: Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) is calling for a delay in Tuesday's Senate GOP leadership elections, injecting another note of uncertainty into what had been a largely foregone conclusion before Republicans' devastating midterm defeat. Why it matters: McCormick isn't demanding that Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) step down. But he is asking his colleagues to pump the brakes on Tuesday's internal elections. - McCormick joins Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) in urging Republicans to postpone the leadership elections. - No one has officially announced a challenge to Thune, who's led the GOP conference since January 2025. But there is clearly growing unease over the conference's plans to move quickly to leadership elections. - Tuesday's elections are still scheduled to proceed, according to a person familiar with the matter. What they're saying: "One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability," McCormick wrote Sunday evening on X. - "A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades. We need a discussion about what went wrong, how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people." McCormick said he had already raised his concerns directly with Thune. - "I don't believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward," he wrote. - "We need leadership in place fast, but Tuesday is too soon. I know it's been the practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it." Zoom out: President Trump clashed repeatedly with Thune throughout the year over the Senate's failure to advance key parts of his agenda, including the SAVE America Act and Thune's resistance to eliminating the filibuster. - Trump renewed his criticism after the midterms, blaming the Senate in part for Republicans' election losses. - "We had a bad election because of a few things. One thing was not getting things approved in the Senate," Trump told reporters.

items.title: Trump backs Nvidia's Huang amid affair, spy investigation
items.excerpt: President Trump defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Sunday night, even as the company's board launched an investigation into his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Why it matters: The blowback to Huang's relationship is only getting more intense by the hour, with multiple members of Congress calling for probes and investors saying the news could put a cloud over the entire AI trade. What they're saying: Trump was asked Sunday night if he's taking Huang with him on an Asia trip next week. - "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him," the president told reporters. - "I haven't heard that he's done anything wrong," Trump added. "He dealt with somebody but, you know, so does everybody else." The intrigue: The New York Times reported in late October that Trump was briefed earlier this year about Huang's relationship with the potential spy but chose not to act. - Huang has been one of Trump's favorite corporate executives since his return to office, with Huang frequently appearing at White House events. - He also traveled with Trump to China earlier this year, even after the reported memo warning the president of Huang's relationship. What's next: A group of House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to agree by Nov. 11 to a date for a briefing on his relationship and Nvidia's national security controls.

items.title: Jeffries backs Hegseth impeachment as Democrats vow probes of Trump allies | Donald Trump News | Al Jazeera
items.excerpt: United States House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has thrown his support behind impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, as the Democratic Party prepares to use its incoming congressional majorities to probe President Donald Trump’s administration. In a Sunday appearance on the Television show This Week with George Stephanopoulos, Jeffries weighed in on the upcoming impeachment resolution, anticipated for the coming days. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.” The impeachment resolution has been spearheaded by outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a vocal critic of the US-Israel war on Iran. “Pete Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries added. “I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution.” ... Both the House and the Senate flipped into Democratic control, with the left-wing party making some of its biggest gains in the lower chamber in more than half a century. ... In Sunday’s interview, Jeffries said the Democratic majority would move “aggressively” in its first 100 days in office, both to address affordability and “unprecedented corruption” under Trump. ... The committee is the chamber’s principal investigative panel, with the power to subpoena ... On Sunday, Garcia told CNN that Stephen Miller‘s influential role in the Trump administration warranted investigation. Miller, who was named last week as White House chief of staff, has been closely associated with Trump’s hardline immigration policies since his first term as president. “What we think is that Stephen Miller is the architect of this horrific, unjust policy happening across the country,” Garcia said, pointing to policies of separating immigrant families and accusations of due process abuses. “Stephen Miller is at the centre of major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and it does deserve oversight and investigation.” Garcia also signalled interest in questioning businessman Elon Musk over his leadership in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a federal initiative that led to widespread federal workforce cuts at the start of Trump’s second term. DOGE also sought access to sensitive government data, including Americans’ personal information. “What happened with DOGE, in particular, and the federal employees losing jobs the way they did and people’s data likely being compromised, I think, is very serious,” Garcia said. Congressional committees have the power to hold hearings, subpoena witnesses, and demand documents, giving lawmakers a constitutional check on the executive branch. The House can also impeach administration officials if a simple majority votes in favour. Conviction and removal, however, require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a high bar even with Democrats controlling the chamber. ... The White House was quick to draw its own battle lines. Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said there could be investigations into Democratic lawmakers over their “threatening” rhetoric. He added he was ready to counter Democratic efforts to probe and impeach Trump officials. “If that’s what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready,” said Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump. “If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It’s me.”

items.title: Trump to meet Qatari prime minister about mediation efforts with Iran
items.excerpt: President Trump will meet the prime minister of Qatar on Monday to discuss efforts to reach a new ceasefire and resume nuclear negotiations with Iran. Why it matters: Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, the key mediator between Iran and the U.S. over the last several weeks, wants Trump to allow more time for diplomacy, sources say. - Trump is still willing to let diplomatic efforts play out and see if a deal is possible. But it is unclear how much time he's willing to give. ... Driving the news: The Qatari mediators — together with other regional players such as Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkey — continued discussions with the Iranians and the White House about a draft proposal calling for a series of steps over two days to build mutual confidence toward a broader deal. - On the first day, the U.S. would lift its naval blockade and release some of Iran's frozen funds. In return, Iran would issue an official invitation to the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to bombed nuclear sites, based on an agreement reached in Cairo a year ago, regional sources said. - On the second day, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen, after which nuclear talks would resume, focusing on Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium. - But the midterm elections have slowed down the indirect negotiations, sources said. State of play: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Iran is still waiting for the U.S. response to the latest proposal.
